question: New Jersey, 1964. A radio horn picks up a faint hiss, 3.5 degrees above absolute zero, that will not go away. Where from?
answer: The afterglow of the Big Bang, stretched into microwaves. Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson did not know it; physicists at nearby Princeton explained it. Two Soviet physicists had even named this very horn, in 1964, as the instrument able to find it. The 1978 Nobel Prize went to the two who heard it.
move: If a signal does not change when you move, it is not coming from nearby.
ask: When something bothers me everywhere I go, have I stopped blaming the places?

clues.text: The hiss is weak and steady, about 3.5 degrees warmer than it should be.
Pigeons nesting in the horn are evicted and their droppings scrubbed out. It stays.
Pointing the horn away from New York City changes nothing.
It is the same in every direction, day and night, through the seasons.

scene.why: The galaxy glows brightest along the Milky Way. A hiss the same everywhere comes from everywhere.

reference: Penzias & Wilson, A Measurement of Excess Antenna Temperature at 4080 Mc/s, Astrophysical Journal 142, 419, 1965; Doroshkevich & Novikov, Soviet Physics Doklady 9, 111, 1964
